newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan digs heels in against army.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan digs heels in against army.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Tuesday dug in his heels against a military challenge to his rule that has strained the unity of his Islamist-led coalition.
"Parliament gives the job of serving the nation to the government and the government is responsible only to parliament," he told a meeting of his Islam-based Welfare Party.
The military-dominated National Security Council (NSC) ordered Erbakan at a weekend meeting to reverse a recent wave of Islamist zeal partly encouraged by his supporters.
Erbakan denied accusations he is trying to turn officially secular Turkey into a strict Islamic state like Iran.
"There is no problem of the system in Turkey," he said. "No one should have any doubts about the system."
Istanbul stocks dropped more than 12 percent by the afternoon and brokers said the plunge was due to political worries and February inflation results that were worse than expected.
Pro-Western partner Tansu Ciller was quoted as saying she would withdraw from the coalition if Erbakan did not try to stamp out Islamist activism soon, as the army demands.
"We are not locked into the government. We will pull out if the conditions require it," the Milliyet newspaper quoted Ciller as telling her conservative True Path Party (DYP) aides.
Ciller did not mention the future of the alliance at a news conference after unscheduled talks with President Suleyman Demirel.
Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, attended last Friday's security meeting but the press says he refused to sign a final statement urging an anti-Islamist crackdown.
Political analysts say he ignores the generals at his peril.
The army, which frequently leads opinion polls as the country's most respected institution, has ousted three governments since 1960.

It practically runs nine mainly-Kurdish provinces under emergency rule in the southeast where it has a free hand against separatist rebels. The armed forces play a major role in Turkey's many disputes with neighbours Greece and Cyprus.
Young officers are taught to idolise Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk, himself a military man.
Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, a member of Ciller's wing, predicted the prime minister could quit rather than disappoint his Islamist backers by heeding the army.
"If Erbakan does not feel the need to carry out the decisions of the NSC, he may resign," Milliyet quoted Aktuna as saying.
The Hurriyet newspaper said other members of Ciller's party wanted to split the eight-month-old coalition straight away.
Despite the friction, there was no immediate sign that Erbakan would lose two parliamentary challenges on Tuesday.
MPs are to gather at 1500 (1300 GMT) to vote on whether to go ahead with an opposition censure motion against the coalition within a week.
Deputies will also vote on opening an inquiry into Justice Minister Sevket Kazan, an Islamist and close aide of Erbakan. Defeat on either issue would be a major blow to the government.
Kazan has been at the centre of a row over Welfare's alleged backing of Sunni Moslem militants.

If accepted, the inquiry would probe alleged abuse of his position for remarks he made suggesting members of the liberal Alevi Moslem sect take part in incestuous ceremonies and a visit he made to a Welfare mayor jailed for organising an Islamist protest also attended by Iran's ambassador.
